headline: Friday night football: Cold Springs wins its way to a home playoff game
summary: Cold Springs and Vinemont won on Friday, Fairview rolled on Thursday, and five other county teams came up short. Here is how every Cullman County team did and where they play next.
body: Cold Springs had the biggest night in the county. The Eagles beat Southeastern 48 to 21 in Bremen behind four rushing touchdowns from Cooper Johnson. The Cullman Times reported that the win, along with other results in the region, locks up the No. 2 seed and the school's first home playoff game since 2003. Cold Springs is 7 and 1 and plays at Carbon Hill on Oct. 23.
Vinemont held on at Glencoe, 28 to 21. The Eagles led 22 to 0 at halftime, Glencoe scored twice late, and a fourth down sack sealed it. Vinemont is 5 and 4 and hosts Susan Moore on Oct. 23.

Fairview played a day early and scored six touchdowns in the first quarter of a 41 to 6 win over Crossville at Dafford Smith Stadium. The Aggies are 5 and 3, are off next week, and close the regular season at Cherokee County on Oct. 30.
Good Hope's six game winning streak ended with a reported 40 to 21 loss at Cherokee County. It was the Raiders' first region loss, and they are 6 and 2. Good Hope hosts Hayden on Oct. 23.

Cullman rallied with 17 points in the third quarter to get within 2 of Parker, ranked second in Class 5A, but Parker pulled away to win 42 to 24 at Woodard Stadium. Cullman plays at Jackson Olin on Oct. 23 at 7 p.m.

Close ones got away from two teams. Holly Pond led 16 to 8 at halftime but lost 17 to 16 at Susan Moore on a late field goal. West Point led in the fourth quarter at Lawrence County before losing 35 to 31. Holly Pond hosts Etowah on Oct. 23 and West Point hosts Deshler that same night.
Hanceville played Thursday because of fall break and lost to Hokes Bluff 49 to 8. The Bulldogs host Oneonta on Oct. 23. You can see every final and next game on our Game Center.

headline: Listerhill Credit Union opens its new Cullman branch and gives $10,000 to Cullman County Schools
summary: The new branch on Industrial Drive SW is open for business, and the credit union marked the grand opening with a big check for the county school system.
body: Listerhill Credit Union celebrated the grand opening of its new Cullman branch on Thursday, Oct. 15, at 702 Industrial Drive SW. Crews broke ground on the building last November, and the staff moved in on Sept. 16.

The best news for local families came at the end of the ceremony. Listerhill handed Cullman County Schools a check for $10,000, and Superintendent Dr. Shane Barnette accepted it for the school system.

City and county leaders turned out for the event, including Mayor Woody Jacobs, Sheriff Matt Gentry, Sheriff elect Chad Whaley, Good Hope Mayor Jerry Bartlett and leaders from the Cullman Economic Development Agency and the Cullman Area Chamber of Commerce.

Credit union leaders noted that the ribbon cutting fell on International Credit Union Day. Listerhill got its start in 1952, when seven workers at the Reynolds Metals plant near Florence pooled $35 so their coworkers could borrow money at fair rates. Today it reports more than $1.5 billion in assets and about 92,000 members.
The Cullman branch is open Monday through Friday from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. and offers lending and mortgage help. You can reach it at (256) 383-9204, and you will find it in our Businesses directory too.

headline: Cullman Therapeutic Recreation invites everyone to a Halloween party on Oct. 24
summary: Costumes, candy, a costume contest and hot dogs from Cullman police officers are on the menu at an accessible party for Therapeutic Recreation members. RSVPs are due Monday.
body: Cullman Therapeutic Recreation is throwing a Halloween party on Saturday, Oct. 24, at 5 p.m., and the theme is simple: everyone belongs here.
The party will be at Palomino RV Resort at Burrow Hamilton Farm, 1315 County Road 222 in Cullman. The resort is ADA accessible, so the evening is built to be comfortable for every guest.

Come in costume, because there will be candy and a costume contest. Officers from the Cullman Police Department will be grilling hot dogs, and Therapeutic Recreation members and resort guests will get a closed trick or treating route of their own so they can enjoy the tradition in a calm, safe setting.

Therapeutic Recreation is the city program that offers recreation and social time for people in our community with special needs and disabilities. The resort, the Cullman Police Department, Omni Sports Academy and Leldon's Locally Curated Goods are helping make the party happen.

Organizers ask that you RSVP by Monday, Oct. 19. The Cullman Tribune story linked below has the email address to use. The party is also on our Events page with directions and an add to calendar button.

headline: Hanceville sibling band Cipollari will play a free benefit show at Terri Pines on Nov. 7
summary: The six Cipollari siblings, the bluegrass band some folks still know as the Cotton Pickin' Kids, are playing a concert to raise money for the Randy Travis Foundation. Tickets are free.
body: Mark Saturday, Nov. 7, on the calendar if you love bluegrass. Cipollari, a band made up of six brothers and sisters from Hanceville, will play "Cipollari Live: A Fundraiser for the Randy Travis Foundation" from 6 to 8 p.m. at Terri Pines Country Club, 700 Pine Hill Drive in Cullman.
Tickets are free, but you do need one. The Cullman Tribune story linked below has the ticket link.

Between them the siblings cover mandolin, two fiddles, guitar, banjo and dobro. Longtime local fans may remember them as the Cotton Pickin' Kids. They released their first album, "Slemish Mountain," in 2020 with a party at Berkeley Bob's Coffee House in Cullman, and two of the siblings now write original songs for the band.

The Randy Travis Foundation was started after the country star's 2013 stroke. The foundation says it works toward a cure for viral cardiomyopathy and helps at risk kids get into arts and music programs, which makes it a fitting cause for a family that grew up playing music together.
You can find the concert on our Events page too, with directions and an add to calendar button.

headline: Monday, Oct. 19, is the last day to register for the Nov. 3 election
summary: Cullman County ballots will carry four statewide amendments and one local question that would freeze assessed home values for qualifying homeowners 65 and older.
body: If you are not registered yet, you have until Monday, Oct. 19, to register for the Nov. 3 general election, according to the Alabama Secretary of State. You can register online at AlabamaVotes.gov or turn in a paper form to the Cullman County Board of Registrars. Polls are open 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Election Day, and you will need a photo ID.

Besides the races, there are five questions on the ballot here. Four are statewide. The Cullman Tribune laid them out this way: one deals with filling a lieutenant governor vacancy, legislative pay and travel spending; one sets up a way for neighboring county school systems to combine; one covers the Pledge of Allegiance and student led prayer; and one would require public schools to play the national anthem at least once a week.

The fifth question is local. It would let homeowners who are 65 or older freeze the assessed value of their home for property taxes. To qualify, the home must be your main residence and you must have lived there at least five years. The bill sets no income limit. Claims would start Oct. 1, 2027, and would be filed in writing with the Revenue Commissioner. Your tax rate could still change, so a bill could still go up even with the freeze.
You can look over a sample ballot on the Cullman County Probate Office elections page before you go. Questions about property tax exemptions go to the Revenue Commissioner's office at 256-775-4776.

headline: Senior Day at the Cullman County Fair is Wednesday, Oct. 21
summary: Folks 55 and older get in free from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m., with free parking and a free lunch for the first 400.
body: If you are 55 or older, plan on the fairgrounds Wednesday morning. The Cullman County Commission on Aging says Senior Day runs from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. on Oct. 21 at the Cullman County Fairgrounds, 1501 Sportsman Lake Road NW.

Admission and parking are free, and the first 400 people get a free lunch. There will be live music in the theater and you can walk through all the fair exhibits. The rides will not run during Senior Day. The Lions Club concession stand will be open if you want something extra to eat.
For questions, call the Commission on Aging at 256-734-1241.

headline: Free Medicare help is by appointment only this year
summary: Open Enrollment runs Oct. 15 through Dec. 7. The Cullman County Commission on Aging will review plans with you, but you need to call ahead.
body: Medicare Open Enrollment started Oct. 15 and runs through Dec. 7. This is the time to switch Medicare Advantage or drug plans, and any change you make starts Jan. 1, 2027.

The Cullman County Commission on Aging offers free counseling, but only by appointment, and it will not take walk ins this season. Call 256-734-1241 to get on the schedule. Spots are limited, The Cullman Tribune reported.

Bring your Medicare card, any other insurance cards and your actual medicine bottles. The office will not accept written lists or pharmacy printouts this year. If you want to be checked for Extra Help, bring proof of household income, including a current Social Security statement.

Rather do it by mail? Call and ask for a packet. It has to be back at the office by Friday, Nov. 13. The Commission on Aging is at 1519 Sportsman Lake Road NW. You can also call the State Health Insurance Assistance Program at 1-800-243-5463 or Medicare at 1-800-633-4227.

headline: West Point and Holly Pond win area titles as volleyball playoffs roll on Monday
summary: West Point, Holly Pond, Fairview, Cold Springs and Vinemont all reached the subregional round, which is set for Monday, Oct. 19.
body: Area tournament week went well for several county volleyball teams, The Cullman Tribune reported. West Point won the Class 4A Area 13 title on its home floor, sweeping Hayden and then beating Fairview 3 sets to 1. It came on the heels of West Point repeating as county champion.

Holly Pond swept every match it played to win the Class 3A Area 10 title at Vinemont. The Lady Broncos beat Hanceville and then swept the host team in the final. Vinemont still advanced as runner up after sweeping Susan Moore.
Fairview got through a five set semifinal against Good Hope and moves on as the 4A Area 13 runner up. Cold Springs finished second in Class 2A Area 9 after losing the final at Carbon Hill.
Cullman, Good Hope, Hanceville, St. Bernard Prep and Cullman Christian are done for the year. Subregional matches are Monday, Oct. 19. West Point and Holly Pond play at home.

headline: Cullman weekend weather: windy and sunny Saturday, chilly nights
summary: The National Weather Service expects sunshine through Tuesday in Cullman, with highs in the 60s to near 72 and lows around 40.
body: Grab a jacket for the morning. The National Weather Service office in Huntsville expects a mostly sunny Saturday in Cullman with a high near 62. A north wind around 15 mph could gust to 30 mph, so hold on to your hat at the ballfield.
Saturday night turns clear and cold, with a low around 40. Sunday is sunny with a high near 66 and a low near 39. Monday warms to about 69 and Tuesday to about 72, both with plenty of sun.
This forecast came out early Saturday, Oct. 17. Forecasts change, so check the Weather Service before you head out.

headline: Hanceville council adds $25,000 for road patching, backs mayor on fire chief
summary: More gas tax money is going toward potholes, a take home vehicle policy is still up for debate, and the council upheld the mayor's removal of the fire chief. The next meeting is Thursday, Oct. 22, at 6 p.m.
body: Potholes were near the top of the list when the Hanceville City Council met on Oct. 8. Council members approved another $25,000 from gas tax money so Public Works can keep patching streets, according to The Cullman Tribune.

The job has turned out bigger than planned. Rusty Fields of Public Works said the damaged spots vary a lot in size and depth, which takes extra time and material. City and county crews are working together at a cost of about $5,000 to $5,500 a day. Fields told the council they are a little more than halfway through.

Take home trucks took up the most time. Councilman Robert Powell has proposed a policy, Resolution 2026-8, that would limit everyday take home vehicles to department heads and employees who are on call. He pointed to fuel, insurance and upkeep, and one estimate put six take home vehicles at roughly $17,000 a year.

Public Works employees pushed back. They said having a truck at home gets them to downed trees, flooding and storm damage faster, and some keep their own tools in those trucks. The council added emergency exceptions and a six month phase out, then held the final vote for its next meeting.

The council also talked about having a say in hiring the fire chief, public works director and park director. Mayor Nolan Bradford said he wants to keep that authority with the mayor. No action was taken.

After about 40 minutes in executive session, the council voted unanimously to uphold Bradford's removal of Fire Chief Chris Hardin, who started in March. The Tribune reported that no reason was given in public and no replacement was named. The Cullman Times reported the vote as well.

A few other notes from the meeting: firefighters answered 116 calls in September, the city gave $500 to the North Alabama Agriplex, Councilman Cameron Rowe joined the Planning Commission, and work is moving ahead on policies needed to bring back a city police department.
If you want to speak up, the next council meeting is Thursday, Oct. 22, at 6 p.m.

headline: Wallace State volleyball has won nine straight heading into Saturday
summary: The Lions swept Bishop State and Lurleen B. Wallace on Friday and finish their home invitational Saturday with matches at 11 a.m. and 3 p.m. at Tom Drake Coliseum.
body: It has been a good fall to be a Wallace State volleyball fan. The Lions sit at 25 and 5 overall and 11 and 2 in conference play after two sweeps on Friday, the first day of the Wallace State Lions Invitational, based on the team's official results.
They beat Bishop State 25 to 9, 25 to 16 and 25 to 11 at noon. That evening they handled Lurleen B. Wallace 25 to 15, 25 to 16 and 25 to 17. That's nine wins in a row.

The tournament wraps up Saturday, Oct. 17, at Tom Drake Coliseum on campus in Hanceville. Wallace State plays Illinois Central College at 11 a.m. and Reid State at 3 p.m. Next week brings two more home dates: Calhoun on Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 5 p.m., and a doubleheader with Southern Union on Thursday, Oct. 22.

headline: Hanceville High's National Honor Society chapter wins national recognition
summary: The Hanceville High chapter earned the National Honor Society's Chapter of Distinction award for leadership and service to the school and town.
body: Hanceville High School has something to brag about. Its National Honor Society chapter was named a Chapter of Distinction, a national honor for students who lead well and serve their community. The Cullman Times and The Cullman Tribune both shared the news.

To earn it, a chapter has to meet every one of the honor society's core standards and shine in areas like student leadership. There is no cap on how many chapters can win, so it comes down to whether a chapter does the work.
Principal Daniel Wakefield gave credit to Ms. Teri Weaver for building “excellent leaders for the real world,” the Times reported. Way to go, Bulldogs.

headline: Oktoberfest drew a record 75,000 people, and Christkindlmarkt is next
summary: Organizers say the four day festival set records for attendance and hotel stays. Christkindlmarkt opens at Depot Park on Nov. 19 with free admission.
body: Cullman Oktoberfest had its biggest year yet. Cullman Parks, Recreation and Sports Tourism told The Cullman Tribune that about 75,000 people came out Oct. 1 through 4, and local hotels had record occupancy.

This was the first year the festival ran through Sunday. Even with a 70 percent chance of rain that day, nearly 10,000 people showed up. Organizers also made more room for craft vendors and say the two headline bands are already booked to come back next year.

Next up downtown is Cullman Christkindlmarkt at Depot Park, Nov. 19 through Dec. 23. Admission is free. Organizers are promising returning vendors, new food and one big new feature they are keeping secret for now.

headline: Cullman police plan tighter safety for races and events after Oktoberfest run
summary: After a resident reported cars driving on the course during the Oct. 3 fun run, the city says future events will be vetted more closely and staffed with more officers.
body: A resident wrote to city leaders after the Oktoberfest fun run on Oct. 3, saying cars were driving along the course and one came within a few feet of a child, The Cullman Times reported. The email came after two other recent crashes near local events, including the death of a woman struck on Highway 31 as she left Oktoberfest on Oct. 1.

At the Oct. 12 council meeting, Councilmember Paul Schaeffer said he had planned to hold off on approving the next race, the Cullman High soccer boosters' Santa Chase. After talking with Police Chief Joey Duncan, he changed his mind. The department now plans a more thorough review of event requests and more officers working each event.

The council approved the Santa Chase 5K, 10K and one mile fun run for Saturday, Dec. 5. Police and Parks and Recreation leaders plan to meet with the resident next month to talk through safety at future events.

headline: Youth Leadership students harvest and cook their own lunch at the Agriplex
summary: Students in the Cullman Area Chamber's Youth Leadership program picked vegetables and cooked a meal in the North Alabama Agriplex teaching kitchen.
body: On Thursday, Oct. 15, students in the Cullman Area Chamber of Commerce's Youth Leadership program got a hands on lesson in where food comes from at the North Alabama Agriplex, The Cullman Times reported.

They pulled sweet potatoes, cut kale and picked purple hull peas. Then they cooked lunch in the Agriplex's new teaching kitchen, with dishes like kale smoothies, roasted sweet potatoes and creamed peas. After eating with the Agriplex staff, they cleaned up and learned how composting works.

headline: Cullman starts work on a long range city plan, and residents will get a say
summary: The City Council hired Goodwyn, Mills and Cawood to guide a new comprehensive plan covering housing, traffic, parking, event space and the kinds of industry the city wants.
body: The City of Cullman is starting on a new master plan, and the council says it wants to hear from you. On Oct. 12 the council approved a contract with the engineering firm Goodwyn, Mills and Cawood to help write it, The Cullman Times reported.

The plan is meant to guide decisions for years on things people deal with every day: housing, traffic, parking, where events happen and what kinds of businesses and industry the city goes after. Council President Kim Hall said it will take a lot of public input for it to truly be the residents' plan. Planning Commission Chairman Michael Sullins said the city will share information so people can take part.

In other business, the council held a first reading on annexing land on County Road 616, set a Nov. 9 public hearing on rezoning land at 455 County Road 587, approved the Santa Chase run for Dec. 5, and approved the Moose Lodge turkey shoots on Saturdays in November and December.

headline: New in town: a downtown boutique, a thrift store and a beignet shop on the way
summary: A Little Too Much opened in the Warehouse District, America's Thrift Stores plans a November opening on 2nd Avenue SW, and Beignets and Brew is coming to Redstone Marketplace.
body: There is something new to shop downtown. A Little Too Much, a locally owned boutique, opened Oct. 1 at 104 1st Ave. NE in the Warehouse District, The Cullman Tribune reported. It carries colorful clothing, vintage finds and handmade items like pillows, purses and jewelry. The owner says new stock comes in every week and the Christmas windows go up Tuesday, Nov. 3.

America's Thrift Stores plans to open in November at 1721 2nd Ave. SW, Suite 1, where Bargain Hunt used to be. No exact date has been posted. The chain sells used clothing and household goods and is hiring for the Cullman store. Its Alabama charity partner is Make A Wish Alabama.

Beignets and Brew lists a Cullman shop as coming soon at 1269 2nd Ave. NW, Suite J, in Redstone Marketplace near 12th Way North. It will have a drive through. Expect New Orleans style beignets, coffee drinks and breakfast croissants. No opening date has been set.

headline: Cullman County CASA is looking for volunteers to speak up for children
summary: Court appointed volunteers help children who have been through abuse or neglect. Training takes four weeks, meeting once a week.
body: Cullman County CASA, short for Court Appointed Special Advocates, needs more volunteers, The Cullman Tribune reported. CASA volunteers are sworn in by a judge and look out for children in court cases involving abuse or neglect, making sure each child's needs are heard while the court works toward a safe, permanent home.

The group recently swore in three new volunteers. If you would like to join, email Cullmancountycasa@msn.com for an application. You will go through a background check, an interview and reference checks, then a four week training that meets once a week.
Not able to volunteer? CASA also accepts donations for school supplies, gifts, hygiene items and other things children need, and it can send a speaker to churches, clubs and community groups.

headline: Good Hope Elementary moves into its new building
summary: The Cullman County Board of Education cut the ribbon Oct. 7 on the new school at 703 County Road 447, and students started classes there Oct. 12.
body: Good Hope Elementary students walked into a brand new school on Monday, Oct. 12. The Cullman County Board of Education held the ribbon cutting the week before at 703 County Road 447, right next to Good Hope Primary, The Cullman Tribune reported.

Superintendent Shane Barnette said Good Hope is growing as fast as any community in the county school system, and the building was placed so it can grow in later phases. Students from each of the seven county high schools helped teachers move in.
Pickup works differently at the new building. Cullman County Schools posted a video on its social media pages showing the new pickup routine.

headline: Cullman High senior named a National Merit Semifinalist
summary: Isaac Heinze is one of only two National Merit Semifinalists from all of the high schools in Cullman County and Cullman City this year.
body: Cullman High School announced Oct. 7 that senior Isaac Heinze is a Semifinalist in the 2027 National Merit Scholarship Program, The Cullman Tribune reported. He is one of only two Semifinalists from all of the high schools in the county and city systems.

More than 1.2 million juniors took the PSAT last year to enter the program, and Semifinalists make up less than 1 percent of high school seniors nationwide. Next comes the Finalist round. About 95 percent of Semifinalists reach that level, and roughly half of the Finalists win a scholarship. Congratulations, Isaac.

headline: City backs road work for a $15 million bank and retail project on 3rd Street SW
summary: The council agreed to pay 80 percent of a turn lane on Highway 278 for a new First National Bank and future retail site at 201 and 401 3rd St. SW.
body: A new bank and a future retail site are planned on about 3.75 acres at 201 and 401 3rd St. SW, and the City of Cullman has agreed to help with the road work, The Cullman Tribune reported. The council approved the agreement Sept. 28.

First National Bank of Pulaski plans a bank and community room at 201 3rd St. SW. The other lot is set aside for retail, though no stores have been named. The whole project is valued at about $15 million.

Under the deal, the city pays 80 percent of a required deceleration lane on U.S. Highway 278 and the bank pays the rest. The agreement does not set a cap on the city's share. Sidewalks are also required, and the city will try for a state grant to help pay for them. No construction or opening dates have been announced.

headline: Put in a storm shelter this year? Apply for the tax credit by Dec. 31
summary: Alabama offers a state income tax credit of up to $3,000 for qualifying shelters, but the application has to reach the state in the same year the shelter goes in.
body: Cullman County EMA is reminding people that the Alabama storm shelter tax credit has a deadline many folks miss. If your shelter was installed in 2026, your complete application must reach the Alabama Emergency Management Agency by Dec. 31, The Cullman Tribune reported. Waiting until tax season can cost you the credit.

The credit covers half of what you spent, up to $3,000. The shelter has to be at your main home in Alabama, installed on or after Jan. 1, 2026, and built to protect against an EF5 tornado. You will need an engineer's sealed spec sheet, proof that it is your main home and a paid invoice.

Once the state approves you, it sends a certificate, and then you file the claim through My Alabama Taxes before you file your state return. The credit cannot lower your tax below zero and does not carry over to another year. Questions go to the Alabama EMA at 205-280-2200.
